candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And they became pregnant, and they bare great giants, whose height was three thousand ells' — the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4 here named explicitly as the half-angelic offspring of the Watchers' union with human women. The 'three thousand ells' (vastly hyperbolic — Charles notes the Greek tradition has lower numbers) signals the disordered scale of the offspring: not merely large humans but a different ontological category, neither fully angelic nor fully human. The Tewahedo theological reading takes this as the prototype of every subsequent demonic infestation: the half-creatures that issue from forbidden union belong to no created order and find their proper place only in destruction.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'The giants turned against them and devoured mankind. And they began to sin against birds, and beasts, and reptiles, and fish, and to devour one another's flesh, and drink the blood' — the violent escalation of giant predation. The four-fold catalog (humans / birds / beasts / fish) traces the giant predation through the whole creaturely order; 'devour one another's flesh' makes them ultimately self-cannibalistic. Tewahedo monastic-ascetic tradition reads this as the ultimate pattern of disordered appetite: unchecked consumption finally turns inward, devouring its own. The catalog itself becomes the textual basis for the standard four-fold dietary categories preserved in monastic fasting rules.
